messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 34, Nathan had been a Navy officer long enough to think of himself as steady under pressure, someone other people looked to when things turned chaotic. The disaster that undid that certainty came during a coastal deployment when a severe storm surge struck with little warning and drove water through the lower levels of the building where he and others had taken shelter. He remembers the crush of bodies trying to force through a narrow passage, the lights failing, and the air turning sour with spilled liquor from a ruptured storage area mixed with seawater and fuel. In his memory the event comes less as a story than as stark, disconnected images: shoulders pressed against him, black water rising, a doorway he could not reach. When it hits him, his body stiffens into the same braced, pinned position he had been in then, as if he is still wedged in place waiting for another wave. At times the memory feels so unreal that he catches himself thinking it cannot have happened to him at all, and that unreality is part of what unsettles him.

In the months afterward, Nathan found that certain moments in ordinary life on base or off duty seemed to seize him before he understood why. A crowded corridor aboard ship, a packed commissary aisle, stepping into a dim room, or returning to physical locations along the waterfront could bring back vivid visual flashes of that night. The smell of alcohol was especially potent; if he passed a bar near the harbor or caught liquor on someone’s breath, he was abruptly back in those images, his muscles locking and his body remembering the posture of entrapment. He began organizing his days around not letting that happen. He waited for empty elevators, avoided social gatherings with friends, and made excuses to leave any place that felt dark, congested, or too much like the places near the flood zone.

As these episodes repeated, Nathan had come to believe that the disaster had permanently altered who he was. He told himself he used to be a happy person but was now miserable all the time, and the contrast felt to him like proof that something essential had been lost. Around other officers, and even at home with his wife, he felt set apart, as though no one else inhabited the same world he did anymore. Crowded places began to mean more than inconvenience; they confirmed his sense that he did not belong anywhere, that other people moved easily through spaces that for him remained charged with danger. That belief made him scan more sharply for dark rooms, tight passageways, waterfront locations, or the smell of alcohol, as if his mind were constantly checking whether the world was about to close in again.

The memories themselves deepened those conclusions. Because what returned were mostly pictures and bodily sensations rather than a coherent narrative, Nathan took their force as evidence that he was still trapped in the disaster somehow. After an intrusive image, he would be left thinking that he was isolated from ordinary life in a way other people could not understand. The strangeness of having a memory that felt both vividly physical and unreal only increased his conviction that he was no longer the same man and could not find a place among others. In turn, when he was already telling himself that he belonged nowhere, the next image came faster and landed harder, as if his own bleak conclusions opened the door for the flood scene to take over again.

He responded by punishing himself mentally. When he canceled on friends or sat alone in the darkened part of the house, he told himself he deserved to suffer because of what had happened. Those private reprimands did not quiet anything; they kept him fixed on the event, replaying the images and bodily terror with even greater intensity. The more he withdrew from friends and avoided circumstances that reminded him of the storm, the smaller his world became. His avoidance brought temporary relief, but it also left him more sensitive to the next crowded briefing room, the next waterfront assignment, the next trace of alcohol in a restaurant, because he was living as if these cues were intolerable. At work, this had started to show. He took longer routes to avoid congested parts of the ship and hesitated over duties in dim compartments, worrying that others would notice.

By the time he sought help, Nathan was frightened by how complete the change felt. His wife had told him he was disappearing from their life together, always finding reasons not to see friends, always on edge about where he sat and what he might smell. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic episode but the accumulation of them: the sense that each avoided gathering, each visual flash, each thought that he deserved his misery was tightening his isolation. What he fears most is that this is permanent—that he will remain cut off, unhappy, and unable to stand where other people stand without feeling trapped. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that the disaster might someday feel like something that happened to him rather than somewhere he is still living.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that triggers or reminders themselves lead to or generate Nathan’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Nathan’s trauma memory or intrusive images lead to increased noticing of, sensitization to, or generation of triggers/reminders.
